# Introduction

Mathematical optimization experiments commonly emphasize solve time, optimality
gap, and solution quality. Energy is increasingly relevant, but it is harder to
interpret because a single process may include model loading, solver
initialization, optimization, and output handling. A credible energy study must
therefore bind measurements to explicit execution regions, record the
experimental context, and reject malformed telemetry instead of silently
repairing it.

Intel Running Average Power Limit (RAPL) interfaces expose model-based energy
information for processor domains and are widely used as an accessible basis
for software energy studies [@rotem2012rapl]. PaScal Analyzer can execute
applications across configurations while collecting execution time, sampled
power, and other performance data [@pascal2026]. The challenge addressed here
is to connect Python solver APIs to PaScal's native manual-region mechanism
without making either the wrapper or the resulting dataset specific to one
solver.

We present PaScal Suite Python, a research prototype that executes Gurobi and
SCIP through a common experiment contract. The work targets four bounded
research questions:

1. **RQ1:** Can both solvers use the same declarative experiment and regional
   telemetry contract while retaining native solver semantics?
2. **RQ2:** Does integrated sampled RAPL energy agree with an independent global
   RAPL measurement within a median absolute-error threshold of 5%?
3. **RQ3:** Do accepted configurations remain within a preferred 10%
   coefficient-of-variation threshold after invalid attempts are disclosed and
   rejected?
4. **RQ4:** Under matched dataset, profile, partition, allocation, and one-core
   conditions, what descriptive time-and-energy differences are observed?

The contribution is the complete measurement and evidence pipeline rather than
a new optimization algorithm. The artifact includes solver adapters, native
region instrumentation, validity gates, provenance manifests, comparison
tables, and a publication workflow. This manuscript consumes previously
generated, checksummed evidence and performs no HPC experiment in continuous
integration.

# Background and Related Work

## Energy telemetry

RAPL was introduced with Intel's Sandy Bridge power-management architecture and
provides energy information for processor domains [@rotem2012rapl]. RAPL values
do not represent complete facility energy, and the domains exposed by a machine
depend on its processor and operating-system interfaces. Consequently, this
study uses RAPL only for the declared PaScal domain and makes no claim about
whole-system energy or carbon emissions.

PaScal Suite combines an Analyzer that executes and measures applications with a
Viewer that explores the resulting data [@pascal2026]. The evaluated Analyzer
supports a global RAPL energy value and a sampled RAPL power series. These two
paths enable an internal consistency check: numerical integration of valid
samples can be compared with the independently reported global energy.

## Solvers and benchmark instances

Gurobi is a commercial mathematical optimization system accessed here through
its Python API [@gurobi2026manual]. SCIP is an open-source optimization suite
centered on constraint integer programming and is accessed through PySCIPOpt
[@bolusani2024scip]. Profile names in this study align experimental intent, not
internal algorithms: defaults, presolve implementations, and warm-start
acceptance remain solver specific.

The workload subset comes from MILPBench, a large benchmark suite for
mixed-integer linear programming [@ye2025milpbench]. We use five hard
capacitated facility-location instances with identifiers 5, 10, 15, 20, and
25. This purposeful subset exercises the complete pipeline but is not a random
sample of MILPBench or of mixed-integer programs in general.

# System Design

The workflow has four layers. First, a YAML document declares the solver,
workloads, resources, repetitions, profiles, telemetry policy, and output
directory. Second, a solver-neutral adapter creates a PaScal Analyzer batch
whose application is a native ELF proxy. Third, a solver-specific Python runner
loads the model, applies a profile, optimizes it, and records metadata. Fourth,
validation tools consolidate the runs, reject invalid telemetry, compare
accepted matrices, and export portable evidence.

The native proxy is necessary because the PaScal build evaluated in the target
environment records manual regions when instrumentation calls originate in the
native process launched by the Analyzer. A guarded inter-process protocol lets
the Python runner request region boundaries without rewriting Analyzer output.
The Analyzer JSON remains the telemetry authority.

Three hierarchical regions are shared by both solvers:

| Region | Operational meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Complete runner pipeline |
| 0.1 | Model read/build phase |
| 0.2 | Solve execution |

The solver profile contract also has three levels:

| Profile | Matched intent |
|---|---|
| default | Solver defaults plus controlled resources and seed |
| presolve-off | Explicitly disable presolve and record the effective setting |
| warm-start | Require a solver-native initial solution and record acceptance |

Gurobi accepts its supported start representations, including MST files. SCIP
uses SOL files, optionally gzip-compressed. The workflow checks file identity
and profile association but does not assume that the two native start
mechanisms are algorithmically equivalent.

# Experimental Method

## Design and controls

The experimental unit is one attempt for a workload, solver profile, and
solver-core treatment. Each configuration has six attempts; acceptance requires
at least five valid attempts. Gurobi was evaluated with one, two, and four
solver cores, whereas the controlled cross-solver comparison uses the one-core
treatment common to Gurobi and SCIP.

Both final campaigns ran on the NPAD `intel-128` partition with exclusive
allocation requested and Slurm reporting `OverSubscribe=NO`. The Gurobi
campaign used source commit `915bd7974edf2a03a279d24a0e3a69dc5f54082f`;
the SCIP campaign used
`b03b6f298db70834192fb499f8fd248e91de22e9`. Manifests record clean tracked
worktrees, Python and package versions, scheduler metadata, configuration
hashes, workload hashes, and initial-solution hashes.

The evaluated environment used Gurobi 13.0.2 and SCIP 10.0 through PySCIPOpt
6.2.1. Version statements here describe the captured campaigns, not the latest
available releases.

## Telemetry validation

For each attempt, validation requires finite, non-negative sampled power,
strictly increasing timestamps, and enough samples to cover at least one
integration interval. Global energy must be finite and positive. Invalid
attempts are preserved in the summary with explicit reasons and are excluded
without correction or imputation.

The sampled whole-program energy is obtained by trapezoidal integration over
the valid power series. Its absolute relative difference from the global PaScal
RAPL value is the energy-consistency error. A profile passes the mandatory
accuracy gate when its median error is at most 5%. Regional energy is integrated
over the union of the region intervals only after the run-level checks pass.
The preferred repeatability gate requires the maximum configuration-level
coefficient of variation to be at most 10%.

For RQ4, duration and energy refer to region 0.2. Energy-delay product (EDP) is
the product of regional energy and regional duration. Ratios are computed as
SCIP divided by Gurobi for matched one-core workload/profile configurations.
The analysis is descriptive: no confidence interval or null-hypothesis test is
reported.

# Results

## Matrix validity

All controlled profile matrices passed the predefined gates.

| Solver | Profile | Valid / attempted | Median energy error (%) | Maximum CV (%) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gurobi | default | 88 / 90 | 0.201043 | 1.450886 |
| Gurobi | presolve-off | 89 / 90 | 0.290858 | 1.877484 |
| Gurobi | warm-start | 90 / 90 | 0.268701 | 1.124702 |
| SCIP | default | 29 / 30 | 0.296794 | 1.654691 |
| SCIP | presolve-off | 30 / 30 | 0.286874 | 0.671986 |
| SCIP | warm-start | 28 / 30 | 0.290148 | 0.746351 |

The observed median consistency errors are below 0.31%, substantially within
the 5% acceptance threshold. The largest observed CV is 1.88%, also within the
preferred 10% threshold. Seven of 360 attempts were invalid: three in Gurobi
and four in SCIP. The invalid-attempt mechanism therefore retained the required
five valid repetitions for every configuration without imputing telemetry.

## Controlled one-core comparison

Fifteen matched configurations combine five workloads and three profiles. The
comparison gate verified matching dataset fingerprints, profile contracts,
partition, explicit exclusive allocation, clean source worktrees, and accepted
input matrices.

| Profile | Median duration ratio | Median energy ratio | Median EDP ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| default | 26.314715 | 26.794993 | 707.638806 |
| presolve-off | 43.115530 | 43.876481 | 1893.048508 |
| warm-start | 9.775579 | 10.186012 | 99.737732 |

A ratio above one means that the SCIP observation exceeded its matched Gurobi
observation. In this bounded experiment, SCIP therefore had higher median solve
duration, regional energy, and EDP for all three profiles. The magnitude varied
considerably by profile, with the smallest ratios under warm start. These
values answer RQ4 only for the declared instances, versions, profiles, node
class, and campaign controls.

# Discussion

RQ1 is supported operationally: both solvers completed the same declarative
profile and region contract, and their outputs passed a common validator. This
is interface parity, not equivalence of solver algorithms.

RQ2 and RQ3 are supported within the measurement design. The two RAPL paths
agreed closely at the profile level, and variability remained below the
preferred bound after transparent run rejection. The fail-closed policy is
important because isolated negative or insufficiently covered sensor series
were observed even in completed scheduler jobs.

For RQ4, the controlled comparison makes the observed ratios eligible for a
bounded performance statement. It does not isolate every causal mechanism.
Different solver implementations, native defaults, start-file semantics, and
campaign times may contribute to the results. The profile-dependent ratios show
why a single aggregate solver ranking would be misleading.

From a technology-readiness perspective, the artifact demonstrates a complete
research workflow in a relevant HPC environment. This supports a TRL 5
prototype and a bounded TRL 6 demonstration of the validated configuration.
It does not establish production readiness.

# Threats to Validity

**External validity.** The evidence covers one benchmark family, five
instances, one cluster, one CPU partition, and recorded solver versions. It
must not be generalized to other MILP classes, hardware, energy domains, or
software versions without replication.

**Internal validity.** Matching the partition and requesting exclusive
allocation reduce interference, while hashes and manifests constrain
configuration drift. The solver campaigns nevertheless ran as separate jobs,
so node-level and temporal effects may remain.

**Construct validity.** RAPL represents processor-domain energy rather than
facility energy. Region boundaries represent the wrapper's operational phases
and may include solver/API overhead. EDP is defined only for the declared solve
region.

**Statistical conclusion validity.** Six attempts per configuration provide
redundancy for invalid measurements but limited inferential power. Medians,
ratios, and coefficients of variation are descriptive; no population
probability statement is made.

**Treatment equivalence.** The profiles match intent, but Gurobi and SCIP
implement defaults, presolve, and warm starts differently. In particular,
solver-native start files need not provide equivalent information.

# Reproducibility and Availability

The repository contains experiment contracts, launchers, validation tools,
tests, and the manuscript source. Raw telemetry, licensed material, benchmark
archives, and large solver-start files are excluded from Git. The evidence
exporter verifies upstream hashes, removes cluster-local absolute paths, and
writes a checksummed portable manifest. The `v0.1.0` software release is archived on Zenodo under the
version-specific DOI
[10.5281/zenodo.22695374](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695374). The concept
DOI [10.5281/zenodo.22695373](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695373) resolves
to the software collection across versions. Repository source and associated
documentation are distributed under the MIT License. The software archive does
not include raw HPC telemetry, restricted solver material, benchmark archives,
or large solver-start files. Checksummed portable evidence is the shareable
archival unit for the validated campaigns.

The manuscript is built with Quarto's manuscript project type
[@quarto2026]. Pull requests render HTML and SBC-styled PDF artifacts, run a
structural PDF regression, and never execute the HPC campaigns. Publication to
GitHub Pages occurs only after merge into `main`.

Software source: <https://github.com/cvictorr2508/pascal-suite-python>.
Permanent software archive:
<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695373>.

# Conclusion

PaScal Suite Python demonstrates that Gurobi and SCIP experiments can share a
declarative, region-aware, fail-closed energy telemetry pipeline on HPC
infrastructure. The controlled campaigns met the predefined accuracy,
replication, and repeatability gates, and yielded 15 matched one-core
comparisons. The results establish an auditable research MVP for the evaluated
environment. Broader claims require additional instance families, systems,
versions, randomized campaign scheduling, and inferential analysis.
